b: Last week, a bunch of readers in a wide variety of jobs shared what you should know about how to get what you need from people in their jobs. Some of the highlights are below, but really the whole post was interesting (and had a particularly large number of submissions from librarians,, health care workers, and educators).

I am a performance engineer for an extremely common consumer product. Among other things, this means that I am responsible for monitoring responses to those surveys you get after you’ve had the product for three months or whatever. We really do read them, and they’re actually quite useful; an uptick in complaints about a specific thing cues us to check in with the manufacturing site to see if there’s an issue. This is one of the ways we catch post-development quality issues.

Please, please, please, be specific in those surveys. “Bad,” “hate it,” and “would not buy again” are not actionable reviews. “Rattles when I do X,” “feels like it’s going to fall apart when I do Y,” “never works when I do Z” help us make the product better.
It takes a long time to fill those things out — if you’re going to take the time, you might as well write something that won’t get ignored!

Former public library staff here: Staff at the desk are there to help you, and are (generally) happy to be asked questions. It is not an inconvenience to them to be asked! It is literally why they are there!

I have met so many people who are reluctant to ask librarians/library staff questions because they worry they’re being obnoxious. Friend, if only you knew how many of the questions library staff get are about email passwords and copy machines. They would love to help you find a mystery book. Or discover why worm bodies can regenerate. Or find your ancestry. Or learn about 19th century sewing methods. Please, please bring the library staff your weird and wild questions.

Tell us. If you don’t like how the medication makes you feel, tell us. If you can’t afford the medication, tell us. If you just forget to take it and so haven’t taken it in five months, tell us. If the therapist we referred you to is a jerk or doesn’t take your insurance or has no availability or is too far away, tell us. I can’t fix every problem that I know about, but I can’t even try to fix any problems I don’t know about.

I work in design. Just tell me what you hate about the thing I made you. Be specific where you can. So many clients don’t tell me the truth because they want to be nice, which is a bummer, because I love making people things they love instead of things they halfheartedly accept, and that’s tough without honest feedback.

I just got out of a call with a client who said, “It feels overwhelming, that’s waaaaay too much text. There’s something about the font … I don’t know how to describe it … I just want something … softer? If that makes sense? And X is more important than Y, so it should come first, we honestly might not even need Y. Sorry to be so negative!” and I was like, “I love you, actually, we should get married and you can give me specific, actionable feedback forever.”

I work for a state legislator, and when you call us for help, we don’t care what political party you belong to, if you voted for us or campaigned for our opponent (or are/were our opponent!), or if you’re 115 and have never voted at all. We are your duly elected representative (and their staff), and our job is to represent you. We will do that. And if the legislative staff from your actual district doesn’t respond, our office will probably help you out even though we’re not your representative, as long as you’re polite. You really can catch more flies with honey, you know.

I’m an office manager. The #1 thing my coworkers could do to make my life easier is to come to me early. You need catering for an event next month? Cool, it’s on the docket. You need catering for an event tomorrow? You better be ready to settle for whatever I can scrounge up in less than 24 hours.

Admins, assistants, receptionists, office managers, all of us can make things happen for you, as long as we get enough lead time! That’s literally it! Of course some times things get sprung on you, and then you have to turn around and ask for that emergency help, but the sooner you tell us what you need, the easier it is for us to make it happen.

I work for a government agency dealing with labor law complaints. I see more and more of them that have these lengthy, Chat GPT-generated explanations of which laws have been violated and the remedy requested that merge together local, state, and federal labor laws in ways that don’t actually apply to the situation or are outdated or inaccurate. You can just submit a complaint saying “I am paid $X per hour” or whatever the issue is, and provide proof, and we’ll figure out if the law has been violated and what to do about it! That’s going to be much easier for everyone than swimming through the soup of an AI-generated legal argument.

Inpatient nurse here: please don’t lie about how much you drink. We’re all going to have a bad time when you’re sweating and shaking on your third hospital day. To us, you look septic. You’ll spare yourself some of the workup (maybe) and get some better medical management earlier in the process if we know you’re probably withdrawing.

A healthcare one: Please don’t get upset when every different area and new member of staff asks you to repeat the same info over and over. It is absolutely frustrating and you’re tired and unwell in some way, but this protects you. A previous person might have missed something in the notes or you might have actually forgotten to say something!

The number of times I’ve seen this conversation play out:
“And do you have any other medical conditions?”
“Nope.”
“And are you on any medications or supplements at the moment?”
” [Laundry list of medications related to diabetes, asthma, hypertension etc.]”
“…”

CPA/tax accountant. Tell us about your major life events! The number of times clients have asked me why their new twins aren’t listed on their tax return is absolutely ridiculous. There is no magic big brother system we plug into to know these things!

I work in communications for local government. We like it when you comment on every post about how our sheriff’s deputies murdered someone. We are cheering you on. Comment on every post. Everyone should know.
And also, if you see a post about vaccines, and you like vaccines, please comment something nice. Please. The anti-vaxxers are SO LOUD.
I’m an EA. You almost certainly don’t want to talk to the execs I support about their calendar or to ask them to attend your meeting/event/conference.

They do not know their own schedule. They will accept things they can’t attend and decline things they could totally make. “Can’t they check their calendar?” They could, but they don’t. “Won’t they just tell you what they agreed to?” They should, but they don’t. They’re insanely busy and in my experience, at least 75% of them have severe ADHD and can’t remember what you said 10 seconds later if it’s scheduling-related.

PLEASE don’t go around a VIP’s EA when it comes to scheduling. I promise you I will do everything I can to make what you need happen, but I have to know what you want from them. They don’t know a darn thing.

Accounting office for a private school): We are very happy to work with parents if things are tight financially due to a layoff/ health crisis/ death in the family/ etc but you have to tell us that there’s a situation. If you ignore our calls/ emails and don’t give any background info, we have no way to know that we need flex the monthly payments to accommodate you.

Volunteering as the receptionist at my local foodbank: When you call your local foodbank/ social services office, the earlier you call, the better. Please don’t wait until your fridge is completely empty, because you’ll have more options if you have some lead time vs needing to find a food pantry today. (Our food pantries have all different days/ hours, so if you call at 1 on Friday you’ll have fewer options.)

Also, if you’re donating food, please for the love of Mike, don’t give super expired food. If it’s recently expired they may be able to take it, but I would call and verify before dropping it off. We have a shrine of the oldest food we’ve gotten – the oldest that came in on my shift was a can of peaches from 1995!

Employee comms person here: if you are coming to me with a request, don’t start with tactics. (“I need a video.” “I need a newsletter.”) Tell me the problem you’re trying to solve and we can discuss the best way to meet your goal.
Addendum from a different commenter: WE NEVER NEED A NEWSLETTER.
Professor working in research. When you reach out with a “cold email,” i.e. you want to connect in some way, maybe you’re a young scholar looking for collaborations or opportunities:

Keep it short and actionable. Present your research in about two sentences. Be as concrete as you can with what you want from me and ask a specific question, such as, “Can we meet?” “Can I come as a visiting scholar on these dates?” or whatever it is.

It is much less likely to go anywhere if you send a looong loong email and are just basically saying “I exist!” I can’t come up with the next step, and I will not read whole paragraphs describing your profile.

I’m a personal assistant in the higher ed sphere; if you need a meeting with one of my scientists, the greatest gift you can give me is clarity about your own parameters. When specifically are you available? Do you want to meet in person or online? What time zone are you in? How long do you ideally want? If I have to come back to you for answers to these questions before scheduling the meeting, it prolongs the whole process and there is a significant chance that you’ll have to wait longer for your meeting, because their calendars fill up bafflingly fast.

Director of finance. Please just talk to me or my team! Lots of people are nervous about money or numbers, and therefore avoid it because they don’t want to look silly or something. I honestly don’t mind what level of knowledge people come in with, or how much hand holding they need. It is literally my job and also one of my major skill sets to find a way to explain it so that you understand. I will keep trying until we get there.

I also don’t mind how many silly questions people ask me. I would far rather be asked than find out six months later that someone accidentally committed fraud because they didn’t want to bother me (no, I am not making this up, this has happened multiple times).

Also, the earlier we know about something the quicker we can respond. Like, if we know six months before year end that there’s going to be an overspend somewhere we can probably make it work, and if there’s going to be an underspend we can reinvest the money into something we need. But if we find out at year end, we’ve missed the opportunity

PhD student…we sometimes get requests to send a visitor to schools/museums/science fairs etc. Usually, the prof who gets the request will pass it on to the graduate students and one of us is happy to volunteer. If you ever need a scientist for something, specifying you’re okay with a graduate student is the best way to get a volunteer!
I’m a local TV news reporter and I could spend an hour on this comment. What comes to mind first:

The thing you want us to cover might not be newsworthy. A “good” story is one that affects a lot of people in the community, evokes a strong emotion, shows people something unusual, is tied to something bigger, etc. I have had a community college get angry that we didn’t report their latest enrollment numbers, a rep from a parking convention (which apparently exists) get angry that we wouldn’t send a reporter to it, and countless people who “founded a nonprofit” (with themselves as the only members) get angry that we wouldn’t do a profile on them. Think about your idea from our perspective, not what is currently mattering a lot to you.
We are very busy! Everyone in this industry is overworked and underpaid, and we have a tenth of the resources we did a decade ago. Please be patient with us.
If you want something covered that is bothering you, be willing to talk about it on camera if that is safe for you to do. We can’t report hearsay. You have a role to play here, too.
If you see us doing a live shot or interviewing someone on the side of the road, don’t honk. You are not being hilarious or edgy. Half the people who passed us before you already did this.
I edited this down, but here’s more from the local TV reporter.

For IT issues, please include what happened and what you expected to happen. I can’t help you if I don’t know what you were going for since that approach might be right for another scenario. Your list of steps is vital, too. Screenshots or screen recordings are also so, so helpful. And if you add what hardware or browser you’re using? Marry me, I’m available Thursday.

I worked as a volunteer at a nonprofit animal shelter as an adoption assistant, so I talked to people about what they were looking for in a pet, introduced them to animals, and helped them complete their adoption paperwork. Something I always tell people who tell me they’re looking to adopt is not to decide what animal to adopt based on how it looks or what you think their personality is like while you’re looking at them in their kennel or shelter space! Talk to the shelter staff about what you’re looking for, what your activity level is, how much experience you have caring for animals, and trust their recommendations.

The biggest thing is that shelters are very stressful environments for most animals, and the behavior you see from a dog or cat in a loud room with lots of other animals and people around or while they’re in a kennel is very likely not what you’ll see when you take them home. As a volunteer, I saw how dogs were when we took them on walks, how they acted in meet and greets, and I knew basically as much as possible about their history. Some dogs would stand at the kennel door barking and looking scary, but when you took them out on a walk or into a quiet meet and greet room they were sweet and calm and loving. Some dogs were paralyzed with fear and lied in the back corner of their kennel barely moving, but when you took them to a play area or on a walk, they were super high energy and excited! You just really can’t judge an animal based on its behavior in a shelter, but shelter staff can usually give you a better idea of what they’re like in a more normal environment.

Also, I know a lot of people believe you can tell a lot about a domesticated animal’s personality based on its breed, but in my experience that’s not really true. It’s definitely the case that some breeds tend to have higher energy or enjoy certain kinds of enrichment, and there are definitely some kinds of dogs we wouldn’t recommend for certain kinds of adopters. But so many people would see a dog of a certain breed and decide it was right for them when we knew it didn’t have the kind of temperament or personality they were looking for or was going to be more work than they were willing to put in. Unfortunately, those were usually the people who ended up returning their animals, which was a bummer for everyone!

So think about what you want in a pet outside of looks before you go to the shelter, and I would say even before you look at or meet any animals, tell the staff or adoption volunteers what you’re looking for and see what animals they introduce you to. Keep an open mind and you will probably leave the shelter with your new best friend, even if it doesn’t look like what you expected!
More very good adoption advice here.

I used to work for a pre-college summer program for high school students (through a nonprofit). Please apply for financial aid if you need it, don’t screen yourself out. You might be right that you won’t qualify, but don’t assume. I’ve had people be accepted and then decline to attend because they couldn’t afford tuition — when they hadn’t applied for aid.

And even more importantly, make sure you apply by the deadline! I would always have people ask for financial aid later (in our case, after they were accepted). By that time, I had much less flexibility with what money might be available.

Tell your therapist the negative or challenging thoughts you have about the therapy itself. That’s your hardest and most productive work. Tell them when you don’t like it. Tell them when you’re not getting what you want. Tell them when you’re ready to move on!
If your therapist can’t handle it, they’re either not doing their work or they aren’t a good fit for you (or maybe … the field). It’s on them to handle your feelings, so tell them the feelings.

Former banker here in the U.S. Please stop saying “this is a stick-up” when you reach the teller. It’s been hundreds of years of banking and it’s still not funny. I have been through a robbery, it’s really not funny.
Speak directly to the deaf person. Do not say to me, “Tell them…” That also means looking directly at the deaf consumer and not me.

I am not their aide, I did not ride with them to this appointment, there are extremely high odds that they are an independent/functional adult, and if they aren’t a functional adult, they probably have an aide with them as well as an interpreter.

Don’t tell me not to interpret something. If I can hear it, the deaf person gets to have it told to them as well. If you want to have a private conversation with someone else, you need to step out of the area.

If a deaf person approaches you in public, like to order a coffee or something, don’t be afraid to try to communicate with them. Write it down on a piece of paper, pull out your cell phone and use a notes app, gesture and point at things, etc. As a sign language interpreter, I am not following around a deaf person all day unless that is what I’m being paid to do that day, and even then, they are more than competent to communicate with you, you just have to be willing to try. Lip-reading/speech reading is very difficult, just write notes to communicate instead of assuming they can lip read.

From the in-patient world of nursing: when you call on the phone to ask for an update on someone, please give your full name and their full name. The number of “can I get an update on my mom?” calls I get is … large. I don’t know who you are or who your mom is! And even if I have a guess, I need to check whether your mom has given permission for us to update you.

Also, no, we do not routinely update people who are named as health care proxies when the patient is totally awake, alert, and updated on their condition. The proxy status applies when you can’t make your own decisions. If the patient is able to make decisions, we won’t be routinely calling you. Request to be part of a meeting with the care team and the patient if the patient wants that.

I manage approvals for a lot of things at my company. If you want me to approve something, give me the info I need up front. If I have to chase you for it, it suddenly becomes much less worth my time to say yes. For example, if you are requesting budget to go visit a customer, then tell me the estimated cost of the flights, rental car, etc. as well as which customer you are visiting and why. I get so many that are like, “I want to visit a customer and am requesting approval.” No further info.

For compliance, please, please come to us when you’re starting to think about doing something. As soon as you think, “I wonder if compliance is going to need to be involved at some point,” send an email or pick up the phone! We can help you so much more effectively if we can help you structure your plan to comply with laws and regulations before you get started, instead of cleaning up a mess after we find out you’ve already been doing it for a year.
